content: Hemoglobinopathies, which include inherited disorders of hemoglobin synthesis (thalassemia) and structure (sickle cell disease), are significant contributors to global morbidity and mortality. According to the World Health Organization, approximately 5% of adults worldwide are carriers of a hemoglobin disorder, with 2.9% being carriers of thalassemia and 2.3% being carriers of sickle cell disease. The global distribution of carriers is influenced by the migration of various ethnic groups. Zinc, a readily available supplement, has been used in intervention programs to address zinc deficiency in individuals with thalassemia or sickle cell anemia. It is crucial to assess the role of zinc supplementation in managing these conditions to reduce complications and associated mortality. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of zinc supplementation in the treatment of thalassemia and sickle cell disease. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Hemoglobinopathies Trials Register, which includes references from electronic databases, journal handsearches, and conference proceedings. The most recent search was conducted on February 1, 2013. The inclusion criteria for the study were randomized, placebo-controlled trials of zinc supplementation administered at least once a week for a minimum of one month. Nine trials were included in the analysis, with data from all nine contributing to the outcomes. Two trials focused on individuals with thalassemia (n = 152), while seven trials involved individuals with sickle cell anemia (n = 307). In patients with thalassemia, one trial found no significant difference in serum zinc levels between the zinc-supplemented group and the control group, with a mean difference of 47.40 (95% confidence interval: -12.95 to 107.99). However, in one trial, height velocity was significantly increased in patients who received zinc supplementation for one to seven years, with a mean difference of 3.37 (95% confidence interval: 2.36 to 4.38) among 26 participants. No significant difference in body mass index (BMI) was observed between treatment groups in another trial. In patients with sickle cell anemia, zinc acetate supplementation for three months (one trial) and one year (two trials) significantly increased serum zinc levels, with mean differences of 14.90 (95% confidence interval: 6.94 to 22.86) and 20.25 (95% confidence interval: 11.73 to 28.77), respectively, among 71 participants. However, there was no significant difference in hemoglobin levels between the intervention and control groups at three months (mean difference: 0.06; 95% confidence interval: -0.84 to 0.96) or one year (mean difference: -0.07; 95% confidence interval: -1.40 to 1.26). Regarding anthropometric outcomes, one trial found no significant changes in BMI or weight after one year of zinc acetate supplementation. In terms of clinical outcomes, the total number of sickle cell crises at one year was significantly reduced in the zinc sulfate-supplemented group compared to controls, with a mean difference of -2.83 (95% confidence interval: -3.51 to -2.15) among 130 participants. However, no significant reduction in crises was observed in the zinc acetate group, with a mean difference of 1.54 (95% confidence interval: -2.01 to 5.09) among 22 participants. Additionally, the total number of clinical infections was significantly reduced in the zinc-supplemented group compared to controls in one trial at three months (mean difference: 0.05; 95% confidence interval: 0.01 to 0.43; total participants = 36) and another trial at one year (mean difference: -7.64; 95% confidence interval: -10.89 to -4.39; total participants = 21). The authors concluded that there is no evidence from randomized controlled trials to suggest that zinc supplementation improves serum zinc levels in patients with thalassemia. However, an increase in height velocity was observed in those receiving zinc supplementation. For sickle cell disease, the evidence is mixed. While zinc supplementation for one year increased serum zinc levels, it did not significantly affect hemoglobin levels or anthropometric measurements. Notable benefits were observed in the reduction of sickle cell crises with one year of zinc sulfate supplementation and in the reduction of clinical infections with zinc supplementation for both three months and one year. These conclusions are based on data from a small number of trials, which were generally of good quality with a low risk of bias. The authors recommend further research on zinc supplementation in thalassemia and sickle cell disease, given the potential benefits observed in these conditions.
